Bifactor Confirmatory Factor Analysis Model

Source: R/fa_bifactor.R
fa_bifactor.Rd

Fits the bifactor model, in which a general factor accounts for what every item of a scale has in common and two or more group factors account for what the items of each subscale share beyond it, with all of the factors uncorrelated (Holzinger & Swineford, 1937; Reise, 2012). The model is described as in fa_confirmatory, by naming the items of each group factor, and is fit by maximum likelihood to raw data (by full information maximum likelihood, the default, or after listwise deletion) or to a covariance matrix. The table reports the loadings, error variances, and intercepts with their confidence intervals; the indices that describe how much of the total score and of each subscale score the general factor accounts for, each with a delta method standard error and a confidence interval (Rodriguez, Reise, & Haviland, 2016): omega and omega hierarchical (omega_H) for the total score, omega and omega hierarchical subscale (omega_HS) for each subscale score, the explained common variance (ECV), coefficient H, and the maximal reliability of each factor, and the percentage of uncontaminated correlations (PUC); and the fit of the model.

Usage

fa_bifactor(
  data = NULL,
  factors,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  M = NULL,
  general = "general",
  general_only = NULL,
  equal_loading = FALSE,
  equal_intercept = FALSE,
  equal_error = FALSE,
  meanstructure = NULL,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "fiml",
  se = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  rmsea_conf_level = 0.9,
  output = c("verbose", "measurement", "summary", "standardized", "fit"),
  ...,
  wald_df = Inf
)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_fa_bifactor'
tidy(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_fa_bifactor'
glance(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A raw data matrix or data frame, rows are respondents and columns include the items named in factors. Supply exactly one of data or S.

factors

Named list of the group factors. Each element names a group factor and gives the character vector of its items; each item is listed under one group factor, and the general factor loads on all of them. Two or more group factors are needed, each with three or more items (two when their loadings are equated with equal_loading); see Details for the structures that are refused. An item, here or in general_only, that is not a column of data or an item of S is refused with an error of class dmar_items_invalid (see dmar_metadata).

S

A symmetric covariance matrix of the items, with dimnames naming the items; N is then required. Supply exactly one of data or S.

N

Total sample size. Required with S; ignored (inferred from the rows) with data.

M

Optional named numeric vector of item means, used with a covariance matrix to model the mean structure (required there when equal_intercept is used). Ignored for raw data.

general

The name of the general factor, "general" by default. It names the general factor's rows (lambda_general_1, omega_H_general).

general_only

NULL (the default), or a character vector of items on the general factor alone, with no group factor: an item written for the construct as a whole, say, or the items of a subscale too small to carry a group factor of its own. They count in the general factor's rows (its loadings, omega, omega_H, ECV, H, maximal reliability, and PUC) and in no subscale.

equal_loading

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element for the general factor and one for each group factor. TRUE constrains the loadings within a factor to a single value. Defaults to FALSE.

equal_intercept

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per group factor. TRUE constrains the intercepts of a group factor's items to a single value; this requires the mean structure. The items on the general factor alone keep their own. Defaults to FALSE.

equal_error

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per group factor. TRUE constrains the error variances of a group factor's items to a single value; the items on the general factor alone keep their own. Defaults to FALSE.

meanstructure

Logical or NULL. NULL (default) models the mean structure exactly when it is needed: under FIML (the default with raw data, so the item intercepts, the nu rows, join the table), when any equal_intercept is TRUE, or when M is supplied. TRUE models the intercepts regardless (raw data or M required); FALSE suppresses them, which FIML does not allow.

estimator

"ML" (default), maximum likelihood, or "MLR", maximum likelihood with standard errors and a test statistic robust to nonnormality (raw data required). Ordered items are not available; see Details.

missing

The missing data treatment for raw data: "fiml" (default; full information maximum likelihood, which uses every case with an observed item; lavaan's name "ml" is accepted) or "listwise". The default is resolved as in fa_confirmatory: with se = "robust.sem" or a test statistic FIML cannot compute, the items are fit as they stand when no item value is missing, and otherwise the call stops and names the option to choose. Ignored with S.

se

Standard error method passed to lavaan. The default, NULL, follows the estimator: "standard" for ML and "robust.huber.white" for MLR. "robust.sem" requires complete data and is refused with FIML, and "none" requests point estimates only.

conf_level

Confidence level of the intervals for the parameters and the indices. Defaults to 0.95. It does not reach the RMSEA interval, whose level is rmsea_conf_level.

rmsea_conf_level

Confidence level of the RMSEA interval of the fit rows, which the rmsea_ci_level row records. Defaults to 0.90, the conventional level, whose limits decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05 (see sem_fit_measures); rmsea_conf_level = 0.95 gives a 95 percent interval. It sets the level in the table DMAR returns and in its glance(); output = "summary" returns the lavaan summary, which shows lavaan's 90 percent interval whatever this argument is.

output

Format of the returned object:

"verbose"

(default) The loadings, factor variances (fixed at 1), error variances, and intercepts, then the indices, then the fit rows.

"measurement"

The indices alone.

"summary"

The summary() of the lavaan fit (not a data frame).

"standardized"

lavaan::standardizedSolution() of the fit; see Details. Under se = "none" its se, z, pvalue, ci.lower, and ci.upper columns are NA.

"fit"

The lavaan fit, which bifactor_indices, ci_bifactor_indices, factor_scores, and lavaan::lavTestLRT() take.

...

For fa_bifactor(), additional arguments forwarded to lavaan (for example cluster); a group argument is an error, as in fa_confirmatory(), and so is ordered. Unused by tidy() and glance().

wald_df

The reference distribution of the Wald intervals and p-values: Inf (the default), the normal distribution, or a single positive number, the degrees of freedom of a t distribution for every parameter and index row (for the indices, on the logit scale), as in fa_confirmatory. The keyword "missing_information" is refused: the calibration study behind it simulated one factor models, and nothing calibrates it for the loadings of a bifactor model or for its indices. It follows ..., so it must be named in full.

x

A dmar_fa_bifactor table returned by fa_bifactor().

Value

For output = "verbose" (default) and "measurement", a data.frame (classes dmar_fa_bifactor, dmar_tbl) with columns syntax, term, estimate, se, test_statistic, p_value, ci_lower, and ci_upper. Its attributes record the model: general, factors, and general_only; equal, a list naming the factors whose loadings, error variances, and intercepts are equated; has_means; omega_metric ("raw_item_sum"); improper, the negative error variances named by item (empty for a proper solution); and wald_df. The verbose table also carries fa_confirmatory()'s test, estimator, missing, fit_indices, and fit_rows. The printed header describes the model, and the lines under the table say what the indices describe. For "summary", the lavaan summary; for "standardized", the standardized solution with the "wald_df" attribute; for "fit", the lavaan fit. tidy() gives the parameter and index rows and glance() one row of the fit rows and what produced them, as for fa_confirmatory.

Details

The model. An item \(i\) of group factor \(s\) is $$x_i = \nu_i + \lambda_{gi} g + \lambda_{si} s + e_i,$$ and an item on the general factor alone lacks the group term. Every factor's variance is fixed at 1 (and its mean at 0 when the mean structure is modeled), every pair of factors is uncorrelated, and the first loading of each factor is freed, so each loading is the covariance of its item with the factor. The general factor carries what all of the items share; a group factor carries only what its subscale's items share beyond that, so its loadings are smaller than those of a factor of the subscale alone, and they can be near zero or change sign when the general factor takes up what the subscale measures. Every loading, error variance, and intercept carries a label, as in fa_confirmatory, and the indices are lavaan defined parameters of those labels, so the fit itself gives each one a delta method standard error. The standardized solution is derived from this fit of the covariances (or of the raw data), with the factor variances fixed at 1, not from a fit to correlations.

Scope and identification. A structure outside the model, or one the data cannot identify, is refused before anything is fit, with an error of class dmar_bifactor_unidentified (which inherits dmar_refusal; see dmar_metadata) that names the factors or items at issue and gives the kind of refusal as its reason element. Fewer than two group factors, and an item listed under two group factors, are outside the model the function fits (reason "scope"): a general factor beside a single group factor, with items on the general factor alone, can be identified, but omega_HS, ECV, and PUC describe how the common variance divides among subscales, which takes two or more. Names placed twice or that coincide are refused with reason "names": an item listed twice under one group factor, or both under a group factor and in general_only; the general factor and a group factor of one name, a factor and an item of one name, or labels made from the names that coincide. A group factor of one item, or of two whose loadings are free (they enter the model only through their product), and two group factors whose general loadings are fixed only up to a scale are not identified (reason "unidentified"). With two group factors and no item on the general factor alone, the covariances between the items of the two groups fix the general loadings of one group only up to a factor \(c\) and those of the other up to \(1/c\), and \(c\) must come from inside a group, whose item variances and covariances must outnumber the group loadings and error variances it estimates. Two groups each of three items (or of two items with equal loadings) leave \(c\) undetermined, and so the model is not identified; an item on the general factor alone, a group of four or more items, equal loadings or equal error variances within a group of three, or equal general loadings each identify it. Every structure with exactly two group factors that is fit gives a warning of class dmar_bifactor_empirical: such a model can be empirically underidentified, since when the item covariances are nearly equal within each group and between the groups, different general and group loadings reproduce them equally well (Green & Yang, 2018). Items on the general factor alone, or items whose loadings differ in strength, protect against it. The identification checks run once the other arguments and the data have passed theirs, so the warning comes only with a fit. A count of parameters cannot see empirical underidentification, and when lavaan's information matrix cannot be inverted, or is singular (scaled to a unit diagonal, its smallest eigenvalue is below \(10^{-6}\)), every standard error, test, and interval is NA, the maximal reliability's included, with a warning. The singularity is checked, as in fa_confirmatory, for the observed information of a FIML fit and for the expected information of a listwise fit or of a covariance matrix alike, since lavaan can invert either when it is singular.

The indices. Write \(\lambda_{gi}\) for the general loading of item \(i\), \(\lambda_{si}\) for its loading on its group factor \(s\) (zero for an item on the general factor alone), \(\psi_i\) for its error variance, and \(v_i = \lambda_{gi}^2 + \lambda_{si}^2 + \psi_i\) for its model implied variance. The variance of the total score, the unweighted sum of the items, is $$\sigma^2_X = (\textstyle\sum_i \lambda_{gi})^2 + \sum_s (\sum_{i \in s} \lambda_{si})^2 + \sum_i \psi_i,$$ and the rows are

omega_<general>

Omega for the total score, \([(\sum_i \lambda_{gi})^2 + \sum_s (\sum_{i \in s} \lambda_{si})^2] / \sigma^2_X\): its reliability with every factor counted as true score (McDonald, 1999).

omega_H_<general>

Omega hierarchical, \((\sum_i \lambda_{gi})^2 / \sigma^2_X\): the share of the total score's variance that is due to the general factor alone, the group factors' variance counted as error. Its square root is the correlation of the total score with the general factor.

omega_<s>

Omega for the subscale score of group factor \(s\), the sum of its items, \((\sum_{i \in s} \lambda_{gi})^2 + (\sum_{i \in s} \lambda_{si})^2\) over that score's variance, which adds \(\sum_{i \in s} \psi_i\): its reliability with both factors counted as true score.

omega_HS_<s>

Omega hierarchical subscale, \((\sum_{i \in s} \lambda_{si})^2\) over the same variance: the share of the subscale score's variance that is due to its group factor alone, what the subscale score says beyond the total.

ECV_<general>, ECV_<s>

The explained common variance, formed from the standardized loadings \(\lambda_{gi} / \sqrt{v_i}\) and \(\lambda_{si} / \sqrt{v_i}\), as bifactor_indices forms it: for the general factor, its share of the common variance of all of the items, \(\sum_i \lambda_{gi}^2 / v_i\) over \(\sum_i (\lambda_{gi}^2 + \lambda_{si}^2) / v_i\); for a group factor's row, the general factor's share of the common variance of that factor's items, the same sums over them, so one minus it is the group factor's own share.

H_<general>, H_<s>

Coefficient H in the form of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016): the closed form of Hancock and Mueller (2001) over the factor's loadings \(\lambda_{fi}\), with every other source of an item's variance (the other factors' included) counted as its error, \(1 / (1 + 1 / \sum_i \lambda_{fi}^2 / (v_i - \lambda_{fi}^2))\).

maximal_reliability_<general>, maximal_reliability_<s>

The maximal reliability of the factor under the fitted model, \(\lambda_f' \Sigma^{-1} \lambda_f\), with \(\lambda_f\) the factor's loadings (zero for an item off it) and \(\Sigma\) the model implied covariance matrix of the items: the squared multiple correlation of the factor with all of the items, the largest reliability any weighted sum of them reaches as a measure of that factor, and the square of the determinacy of the factor's regression score. H treats the variance an item shares with the other factors as uncorrelated error, which in a bifactor model it is not, so the two differ, in either direction; bifactor_indices says when.

PUC_<general>

The percentage of uncontaminated correlations, as a proportion: the share of the pairs of items that do not share a group factor, whose correlations reflect the general factor alone. It depends on the structure, not on the data, so it has no standard error or interval.

Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) describe how each is read. In brief, omega_H against omega for the total score says how much of the total score's reliable variance is general; omega_HS against omega for a subscale says how much of the subscale score's reliable variance is its own; ECV and PUC describe how close the items are to measuring one thing; and H and the maximal reliability describe how well a factor could be measured by an optimally weighted composite. The table reports the numbers with their uncertainty; whether a total or subscale score is worth reporting is the researcher's judgment, and the package draws no line.

The metric of omega. Omega, omega_H, and omega_HS here are the reliabilities of unit-weighted sums of the items as they are scored, the coefficients that fa_confirmatory and semTools::compRelSEM() compute. bifactor_indices computes them from the standardized solution, for sums of the standardized items, as Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) write them. The two agree when the items have equal variances and differ otherwise: on the example below, whose tests' variances range from 8.0 to 153.3, omega_H is 0.552 for the sum of the scores and 0.577 for the sum of the standardized scores, and on the simulated example of bifactor_indices, whose items have nearly equal variances, 0.67305 against 0.67348. ECV is formed from the standardized loadings, and H, the maximal reliability, and PUC do not depend on the metric of the items, so those rows equal bifactor_indices's with its model implied denominator. With output = "standardized", the defined indices are evaluated at the standardized parameters, so the omega rows there are those of the standardized items. lavaan evaluates a defined parameter at the standardized values of the labels it names, and a label that equal_loading or equal_error gives several items has one unstandardized value but a standardized value for each item, which differ when the items' variances differ; lavaan uses the first item's. Each index that uses such a label is computed here from every item's own standardized loadings and error variance, as fa_confirmatory computes its rows, with a delta method standard error from their derivatives with respect to the free parameters and lavaan's covariance matrix of the estimates (under se = "bootstrap", from lavaan's bootstrap draws); the other indices are lavaan's. ECV and H then equal the rows of the other tables.

Intervals. The standard errors of omega, omega_H, omega_HS, ECV, and H are lavaan's delta method standard errors of the defined parameters. The maximal reliability needs a matrix inverse, which lavaan's defined parameters cannot express, so its standard error is the delta method's with the derivatives taken numerically over the free parameters and lavaan's covariance matrix of their estimates, as fa_exploratory forms those of its determinacies. For every index the limits are formed on the logit scale from that standard error and transformed back (Browne, 1982; the confidence interval transformation principle of Kelley, 2007), as fa_confirmatory forms the limits of omega and H, so they lie within (0, 1); the se column is the standard error of the index itself. The sample values of H and of the maximal reliability overstate their population values on average, the more so for a weakly determined factor (Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, & McIntosh, 2019); ci_bifactor_indices on the fit of output = "fit" gives bootstrap intervals for the indices of bifactor_indices and the bootstrap estimate of that bias.

Improper solutions. A bifactor model often gives an improper solution, an error variance estimated below zero, and the estimate is one of two kinds. It can be a finite maximum of the likelihood: on holzinger_swineford, nine tests in three groups of three (visual perception, cubes, and lozenges; paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning; addition, counting groups of dots, and straight and curved capitals) give visual perception an error variance of -41, and the likelihood falls on either side of that value. Such a solution is reported. The maximal reliability is not defined for it, and neither is H for a factor on which an item's standardized loading reaches one, nor an omega whose items' error variances sum below zero; those rows are NA, with a warning that names the items (beside the warning of class dmar_heywood_warning that fa_confirmatory gives), and the improper attribute holds the negative error variances. The other rows are reported as estimated, and an improper solution's indices are better read as a sign that the model asks more of the data than they hold. Or the likelihood can have no maximum at all. With a fourth group factor on the Woody-McCall mixed fundamentals, revised paper form board, and flags tests beside those three groups, the residual covariances of the fourth group's tests, beyond the general factor, are all negative, which no group factor can reproduce (a single factor implies three covariances whose product is not negative), and the likelihood keeps rising, toward a limit, as the error variance of the paper form board falls without bound. lavaan's optimizer stops at -1163 under FIML, where its steps stop gaining, a point set by its starting values and tolerance rather than by the data, and every index read there would describe the optimizer. So when an error variance is negative, the function fits the model again with it held further out (at ten times its estimate, or one model implied variance below it, whichever is further), and when the log likelihood there is higher, or lower by no more than \(10^{-6}\) per case (a likelihood that flat leaves the estimate as much to where the optimizer stopped as a ridge does), it stops, for every output ("fit" included), with an error of class dmar_no_maximum (see dmar_metadata) that names the test and prints the lavaan code of the fit; there, bounds = "pos.var" (which holds every error variance at zero or above, and which ... passes on from here as well) or a different model, such as one with the covariances of the group's items freed in place of the group factor, are the choices.

Ordered items. fa_bifactor() fits continuous items, and ordered is refused. Fit the model to ordered items with lavaan::cfa() (ordered = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE, std.lv = TRUE) and pass the fit to bifactor_indices, which reports the indices on the metric of the latent responses behind the categories; the bifactor coefficients of a sum of the observed categories are not implemented.

The other bifactor functions. output = "fit" returns the lavaan fit, so the same model feeds bifactor_indices, which reports the indices on the standardized metric, without intervals, and can take the observed composite variance as the denominator, and ci_bifactor_indices, which gives them bootstrap intervals, an alternative to the delta method intervals here that does not rest on the normal approximation and that sets improper replications aside.

Row names under term: lambda_<factor>_<j> (loadings, the general factor's numbered over every item, the items of the group factors in their order and then those of general_only; lambda_<factor> when equated), phi_<factor> (the factor variances, fixed at 1), psi_<factor>_<j> and nu_<factor>_<j> (the error variances and intercepts of a group factor's items; psi_<general>_<j> and nu_<general>_<j> for an item on the general factor alone, numbered as its general loading), the indices above, and fa_confirmatory's fit rows chi_square through H1, whose versions and the lines under the table are as there.

References

Aguirre-Urreta, M. I., Rönkkö, M., & McIntosh, C. N. (2019). A cautionary note on the finite sample behavior of maximal reliability. Psychological Methods, 24(2), 236–252. doi:10.1037/met0000176

Browne, M. W. (1982). Covariance structures. In D. M. Hawkins (Ed.), Topics in applied multivariate analysis (pp. 72–141). Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press.

Green, S., & Yang, Y. (2018). Empirical underidentification with the bifactor model: A case study. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 78(5), 717–736. doi:10.1177/0013164417719947

Hancock, G. R., & Mueller, R. O. (2001). Rethinking construct reliability within latent variable systems. In R. Cudeck, S. du Toit, & D. Sörbom (Eds.), Structural equation modeling: Present and future (pp. 195–216). Scientific Software International.

Holzinger, K. J., & Swineford, F. (1937). The bi-factor method. Psychometrika, 2(1), 41–54. doi:10.1007/BF02287965

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

McDonald, R. P. (1999). Test theory: A unified treatment. Erlbaum.

Reise, S. P. (2012). The rediscovery of bifactor measurement models. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 47(5), 667–696. doi:10.1080/00273171.2012.715555

Rodriguez, A., Reise, S. P., & Haviland, M. G. (2016). Evaluating bifactor models: Calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychological Methods, 21(2), 137–150. doi:10.1037/met0000045

fa_confirmatory for the correlated factors model of the same items; fa_second_order for the second-order model whose first-order factors are the group factors, which is nested in the bifactor model; bifactor_indices and ci_bifactor_indices for the indices of a fitted bifactor model on the standardized metric and their bootstrap intervals; factor_scores for the factor scores and their determinacy; reliability_omega and reliability_H.

Examples

data(holzinger_swineford)
hs_groups <- list(
  spatial = c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t3_paper_form_board",
              "t4_lozenges"),
  verbal  = c("t5_general_information", "t6_paragraph_comprehension",
              "t7_sentence", "t8_word_classification", "t9_word_meaning"),
  memory  = c("t14_word_recognition", "t15_number_recognition",
              "t16_figure_recognition", "t17_object_number",
              "t18_number_figure", "t19_figure_word"))

# A general factor on the 15 tests and three group factors: the
# indices, each with a delta method interval.
fa_bifactor(holzinger_swineford, hs_groups, output = "measurement")

generics::glance(fa_bifactor(holzinger_swineford, hs_groups))
#>   chi_square df     p_value      cfi       tli      rmsea  rmsea_low rmsea_high
#> 1   122.7287 75 0.000423185 0.969631 0.9574834 0.04598074 0.03067577 0.06031208
#>         srmr      AIC      BIC    logLik estimator missing     test fit_indices
#> 1 0.04394018 27584.12 27806.55 -13732.06        ML    fiml standard      robust
#>   rmsea_ci_level h1_diagnostic wald_calibration_note
#> 1            0.9          <NA>                  <NA>

# The lavaan fit feeds bifactor_indices(), whose omega, omega_H, and
# omega_HS describe sums of the standardized tests (0.577 for omega_H,
# against 0.552 for the sum of the scores above).
fit <- fa_bifactor(holzinger_swineford, hs_groups, output = "fit")
bifactor_indices(fit)
#>  factor  ECV   omega omega_H omega_HS PUC   H    
#>  general 0.407 0.878 0.577   <NA>     0.705 0.789
#>  spatial 0.626 0.678 <NA>    0.256    <NA>  0.393
#>  verbal  0.330 0.915 <NA>    0.612    <NA>  0.823
#>  memory  0.382 0.728 <NA>    0.455    <NA>  0.624
#> 
#> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model
#> 
#> For a group factor, ECV is the general factor's share of the common variance of that factor's items (one minus it is the group factor's share), and omega is the reliability of their total score
#> H is the index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016), which counts the other factors' common variance as uncorrelated error; the maximal reliability the fitted model implies is general 0.681, spatial 0.362, verbal 0.780, memory 0.595 (attribute "maximal_reliability"; ci_bifactor_indices() gives each an interval)
